line coding: The process of converting digital data to digital signal: a sequence of bits is converted to a digital signal. An encoder does it at the sender and a decoder re-creates the data at the receiver. See [Line coding](#/comp3721-w4/line-coding-elements).
data element|bit: The smallest entity that can represent a piece of information. Two types, 0 and 1. Data elements are what we need to send (logically). See [Line coding](#/comp3721-w4/line-coding-elements).
signal element|symbol|state: The shortest unit (timewise) of a digital signal; it carries data elements. Signal elements are what we can send (physically). See [Line coding](#/comp3721-w4/line-coding-elements).
r|ratio: The number of data elements carried by each signal element, different for each line coding scheme. Slide figures: $1$, $1/2$, $2$, $4/3$. NRZ schemes and AMI have $r = 1$; the Manchester schemes have $r = 1/2$. See [Line coding](#/comp3721-w4/line-coding-elements).
N|data rate|bit rate: The number of data elements (bits) sent in 1 second, in bps. An increase in the data rate is an increase in the speed of transmission. See [Data rate & signal rate](#/comp3721-w4/data-rate-signal-rate).
S|Savg|signal rate|baud rate|modulation: The number of signal elements sent in 1 second, in baud. $S = N / r$, and on average $S = c \times N \times \frac{1}{r}$. A decrease in the signal rate is a decrease in the bandwidth requirement. See [Data rate & signal rate](#/comp3721-w4/data-rate-signal-rate).
baud: The unit of the signal rate: signal elements per second. The data rate is in bps. See [Data rate & signal rate](#/comp3721-w4/data-rate-signal-rate).
c|case factor: The factor in $S = c \times N \times \frac{1}{r}$, different for each case: worst (maximum signal rate), best (minimum signal rate), average. The slide example uses $c = 1/2$. See [Data rate & signal rate](#/comp3721-w4/data-rate-signal-rate).
B|bandwidth: For a digital signal the baud rate, not the bit rate, determines the required bandwidth: $B = c \times N \times \frac{1}{r}$. The actual bandwidth is infinite; the effective bandwidth is finite. See [Bandwidth of a digital signal](#/comp3721-w4/digital-bandwidth).
Nmax: The maximum data rate of a channel: $N_{max} = \frac{1}{c} \times B \times r$, which is the Nyquist formula $2 \times B \times \log_{2} L$ when each level is one signal element and $c = 1/2$. See [Bandwidth of a digital signal](#/comp3721-w4/digital-bandwidth).
L: The number of signal levels. A signal with $L$ levels can carry $\log_{2} L$ bits per level, so $r = \log_{2} L$ when each level is one signal element. See [Bandwidth of a digital signal](#/comp3721-w4/digital-bandwidth).
baseline: The running average of the received signal power that the receiver calculates. The incoming signal power is evaluated against it to determine the value of the data element. See [Baseline wandering & DC components](#/comp3721-w4/baseline-dc).
baseline wandering: A drift in the baseline caused by a long string of 0s or a long string of 1s. It makes the received signal difficult to decode; a good line coding scheme needs to prevent it. See [Baseline wandering & DC components](#/comp3721-w4/baseline-dc).
DC component|DC components: The very low frequencies (around zero) created by a duration of fixed voltage level in a digital signal. As a bias it is the mean amplitude of the waveform; a mean of zero is DC balanced (DC free). A problem for a system that cannot pass low frequencies or uses electrical coupling. See [Baseline wandering & DC components](#/comp3721-w4/baseline-dc).
self-synchronization|clock recovery: A self-synchronizing digital signal includes timing information in the data being transmitted: transitions that alert the receiver to the beginning, middle, or end of the pulse and can reset its clock. The 04a note calls it clock recovery. See [Self-synchronization](#/comp3721-w4/self-synchronization).
unipolar|on-off keying: A scheme with all the signal levels on one side of the time axis, either above or below. Unipolar NRZ: positive voltage for 1, zero voltage for 0. See [Unipolar and polar NRZ](#/comp3721-w4/unipolar-polar-nrz).
NRZ: Non-return-to-zero: the signal does not return to zero at the middle of the bit. See [Unipolar and polar NRZ](#/comp3721-w4/unipolar-polar-nrz).
polar: A scheme whose voltages are on both sides of the time axis: NRZ, RZ, and biphase (Manchester, and differential Manchester). See [Unipolar and polar NRZ](#/comp3721-w4/unipolar-polar-nrz).
NRZ-L: NRZ-Level: two levels of voltage amplitude, positive for 0 and negative for 1 (slide 55). See [Unipolar and polar NRZ](#/comp3721-w4/unipolar-polar-nrz).
NRZ-I: NRZ-Invert: the change or lack of change in the level of the voltage determines the value of the bit. No change for 0 and change for 1. See [Unipolar and polar NRZ](#/comp3721-w4/unipolar-polar-nrz).
biphase: The slide's group name for Manchester and differential Manchester: every bit has a transition at its middle. See [Manchester](#/comp3721-w4/manchester).
Manchester: 0 is high-to-low and 1 is low-to-high, with the transition at the middle of the bit (slide 57). Used for IR protocols, RFID and NFC. Two signal elements per bit. See [Manchester](#/comp3721-w4/manchester).
differential Manchester: Always a transition at the middle of the bit; at the start of the bit, inversion for 0 and no inversion for 1. Used in 802.5 with twisted pair. See [Manchester](#/comp3721-w4/manchester).
differential encoding: The slide's class for NRZ-I and differential Manchester: the bit is read from a change or lack of change, not from the level. See [Manchester](#/comp3721-w4/manchester).
bipolar|multilevel binary: A scheme with three voltage levels: positive, negative, zero. One data element is at zero and the other alternates between positive and negative. See [Bipolar AMI](#/comp3721-w4/bipolar-ami).
AMI: Alternate Mark Inversion (alternate 1 inversion): 0 is a neutral zero voltage, 1 is alternating positive and negative voltages. See [Bipolar AMI](#/comp3721-w4/bipolar-ami).
